chunks.content: 1 Introduction The diagnosis of Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria (PNH) relies on detecting the loss of the glycosyl‐phosphatidyl inositol (GPI)‐anchored surface molecules from both white blood cells (WBCs) and red blood cells (RBCs) by flow cytometry [ , , ], despite the underlying molecular mechanism involving somatic mutations of the X‐linked phosphatidyl‐inositol glycan Class A ( PIGA ) gene [ , ]. Significant progress has been made since the use of the FLAER reagent [ , ] and the publication of international recommendations [ , , , , ]. Various sizes of the PNH clone, consisting of totally deficient cells (type III) alone or associated with partially deficient cells (type II) [ ], can be quantified by flow cytometry. The International PNH Interest Group (IPIG) has classified disease with PNH clones into three subtypes: classical PNH, which includes hemolytic and thrombotic patients who have evidence of PNH clones in the absence of another bone marrow failure disorder; PNH in the context of other primary bone marrow disorders, such as aplastic anemia and myelodysplastic neoplasms; and subclinical PNH, in which patients have small PNH clones but no clinical or laboratory evidence of hemolysis or thrombosis [ ]. Patients with classical PNH typically have higher clone sizes in WBCs; monocyte and neutrophil clone sizes classically correlate well at the time of diagnosis than patients in other categories; these patients also, by definition, have evidence of hemolysis in the form of elevated LDH and reticulocyte counts. RBC clone sizes, however, are less reliable as these are typically lower in untreated patients with PNH due to hemolysis and/or transfusion. Importantly, the size of the neutrophil clone is relevant to the thrombosis risk for the classical PNH patient [ ]. Patients with subclinical PNH have the smallest clone sizes of any of the IPIG classification groups [ , , , , , ]. Early diagnosis of PNH is essential for providing optimal care and treatment if clinically indicated [ , , , , ]. Since flow cytometry is the gold standard to detect PNH clones, performing the assay on fresh cells is crucial to ensure high‐quality results. Therefore, the French PNH working group, initiated in 2010 after the publication of the first international recommendations [ ], aimed to harmonize diagnostic practices throughout the country. First, a dedicated workshop was conducted to evaluate different flow cytometry methods in a multiplatform and multicenter approach. Then, we developed in 2013 a quality control scheme for the French‐speaking region based on the international recommendations for PNH screening [ ]. This interlaboratory comparison program is still ongoing, and we report here on our group's 10‐year experience, during which we successfully built a strong network of cytometrists. 2 2010—The Start With a Dedicated Workshop for <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">PNH</styled-content> Testing on <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">WBCs</styled-content> In 2010, the first publication of the international recommendations highlighted the relevance of a new reagent for flow cytometry called FLAER, an inactivated bacterial toxin able to bind to all GPI‐anchored proteins on leucocytes and to detect their deficiency [ , , ]. In order to share these guidelines, the French PNH working group was established in 2010. Inspired by the General de Gaulle's famous “18th of June Call,” we initiated a dedicated workshop following our call on June 18, 2010, marking the first French‐speaking meeting focused on PNH diagnosis and high‐sensitivity assays in WBCs. Thirty‐five French and Belgian laboratories participated in this multicenter study aimed at evaluating various flow cytometry methods for PNH testing on WBCs across multiple platforms. 2.1 Succeeding in Multicenter Instrument Harmonization The 35 centers were equipped with multiparameter flow cytometers including 8‐color/3‐laser FACSCanto II (BD Biosciences, San Jose CA, USA) in 14 laboratories, 5‐color/1‐laser FC500 (Beckman‐Coulter, Miami FL, USA) in 13 laboratories, and 10‐color/3‐laser Navios (Beckman‐Coulter) in 8 laboratories. The harmonization of the instrument settings was achieved in the 18 centers outfitted with 3‐laser flow cytometers using 8‐peak Rainbow bead calibration particles, after conversion of the fluorescent intensity target values [ ] (Figure ). As an illustration, the coefficients of variation (CVs) were below 5% for FITC, PE, PerCP‐Cy5.5/PC5.5, APC, and V450/PB fluorescence channels, yet slightly increased for the PE‐Cy7 channel to 5.7%, as expected [ ]. 2.2 Achieving a 10<sup>−4</sup> Limit of Detection in a Harmonized Multicenter Approach In order to investigate the technical limit of PNH testing in a multicenter approach, the participating centers were asked to perform three different staining procedures on WBCs, after implementing the harmonization described above. At that time, neither panel option included CD64 for monocyte gating. The gating strategy used was the one recommended by the international guidelines [ ]. The purpose of that workshop was to develop a high‐sensitivity test dedicated to WBCs in a harmonized multicenter approach. In this study, the minimal requirements for defining a PNH population were the observation of at least 20 events with total absence of GPI‐linked protein expression (type III cells). Hence, all participants were asked to acquire a minimum of 200,000 neutrophils in order to reach the optimal limit of detection. Three hundred and five peripheral blood samples were obtained from 75 locally diagnosed PNH patients (PNH clones ranging from 0.08% to 99.95%), 62 patients with circulating immature granulocytes, and 41 patients with MDS, as well as 127 controls. The initial results gathered from in‐house gating strategies highlighted the need for harmonized procedures and participant education, which were subsequently implemented. A higher cellular background was observed in MDS samples and in those with immature granulocytes. By employing harmonized multiparametric approaches with both 6‐color combinations and harmonized gating strategies procedures across multiplatforms, we achieved a 10 −4 limit of detection [ ]. For robust quantification of minor PNH clones, the use of the FLAER is recommended [ ]. This reagent was included in all the files generated for our interlaboratory comparison program (see below). 3 2013–2024—Highlights From the 10‐Year Experience of <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">PNH</styled-content> Interlaboratory Comparison Program The insights gained from the workshop highlighted that, for PNH diagnosis by flow cytometry, both technical proficiency and the accuracy of interpretation and reporting are equally critical. UK NEQAS for Leucocyte Immunophenotyping proposes stabilized samples for PNH in their External Quality Assessment (EQA) programs [ , ]. However, there was a need for a French‐speaking program, particularly for the report drafting. Therefore, we have developed since 2013 a quality control scheme for the French‐speaking region, aligned with the first international guidelines for PNH screening [ ]. This program aims to improve PNH diagnosis practices by analyzing the three recommended different populations in peripheral blood: neutrophils, monocytes, and RBCs. 3.1 Proposing a Two‐Step Survey Program We propose a 1‐year, two‐step survey program to any volunteering clinical laboratories from French‐speaking countries [ ]. It consists of running two successive surveys: a virtual survey based on raw data file analysis to harmonize data interpretation and quality of reports, and a second survey based on a fresh whole‐blood sample analysis to examine the whole process, from the technical procedure to the final report, and appreciate the employed methods in the participating laboratories. Regarding virtual cases, raw data files sent to the centers are currently generated simultaneously by different cytometers: BD Biosciences instruments (BD FACSCanto II and FACSLyric, this latter being used since 2021) and Beckman Coulter instruments (Navios and DxFLEX, this latter being used since 2023). In the context of the fresh survey, whole blood samples are provided by Dr. Bernard Drenou (Groupe Hospitalier de la Région Mulhouse Sud Alsace) in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki, and participants are asked to use their own routine flow cytometric procedures immediately after reception. Following the international guidelines [ ], participants are instructed to report the PNH clone size as follows: only the total PNH clone size in both the WBCs (neutrophils and monocytes) should be included in the conclusion, alongside the percentage of type II and type III RBCs and the total RBC clone size. In France, data on type II and type III percentages in WBCs are also collected, along with type II and type III percentages in RBCs, due to the establishment of the National Observatory of PNH clones. It is important to note that in cases where there is no clear distinction between PNH type II and type III RBCs, it is recommended to report a combined population of RBCs with CD59 deficiency, accompanied by a comment explaining the reason, rather than setting arbitrary regions for type II and type III [ ]. For the statistical analysis of the participant results, a robust statistical method is used in compliance with the ISO/International Electrotechnical Commission 17043 [ ] requirement concerning the proficiency of the interlaboratory quality controllers. Robust mean, coefficient of variation (CV), standard deviation (SD), and z score are calculated for type II, type III, and total PNH cell subsets across the three analyzed lineages (neutrophils, monocytes, and RBCs). Robust mean, coefficient of variation (CV), standard deviation (SD), and z score are calculated for type II, type III, and total PNH cell subsets across the three analyzed lineages (neutrophils, monocytes, and RBCs). These metrics are provided to each participant in a private report for both virtual and fresh cases with a PNH clone. In case where no PNH clone is detected, only the robust mean, CV, and SD of the number of analyzed cells are provided, along with the assay sensitivity for the three different lineages included. All private reports incorporate a standard interpretation of the results developed by the group of experts. Eventually, the participants also receive a general report on each of the two different surveys [ ]. 3.2 Demonstrating the Strong Commitment From French‐Speaking Laboratories Throughout the 10‐Year Program The first 2013 edition of the interlaboratory comparison program succeeded in rallying 49 participants from voluntary centers [ ]. Over the last 10 years, the number of participants slightly increased (Figure ), achieving nearly 60 participants in 2023, including the four expert centers: 50 French metropolitan, one French overseas, four Belgian, one Swiss, and one Moroccan (Figure ). This demonstrates a strong commitment from the registered centers throughout the program duration. We believe that this participant engagement relies on both the quality of the flow cytometry files provided and the diverse PNH clinical situations that illustrate “real‐life” issues. Over the past 10 years, nine fresh cases (FC) were provided to the participants (Figure ), featuring various clone sizes across the three lineages, ranging from 0.15% to 98.8% on neutrophils. We collected the mean and the coefficient of variation for each survey (Table ). Regardless of the lineage, smaller clone sizes are associated with a wider coefficient of variation. Notably, the percentage of type II RBCs, ranging from 0.03% to 7.42%, is often associated with a very large coefficient of variation, highlighting the challenges in delineating this cell type, as it has been elegantly recently demonstrated [ ]. 3.3 Offering Insights Into Various <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">PNH</styled-content> Clinical Situations The interlaboratory comparison program has evolved over the last 10 years, particularly to align with the revised international guidelines [ , , , ]. New panels for WBC analysis of virtual cases were proposed, notably for monocyte gating. CD64 has been defined as the recommended non‐GPI linked marker for monocyte identification instead of CD33. Therefore, we chose to modify in 2019 the staining of the samples used for the virtual cases and have since proposed panels that include either CD64 or CD33. However, we decided not to implement CD157, despite its potential to replace both CD24 and CD14 [ ], since several CD157‐negative, non‐PNH cases have been reported [ ]. Besides, owing to the strong emphasis placed on the RBC analysis in the revised recommendations, we proposed cases focusing on the importance of studying that lineage. Indeed, we proposed a virtual case involving a 70‐year‐old woman with aplastic anemia. The assay sensitivity on monocytes did not allow for a conclusion, while GPI‐deficient cells were detected in neutrophils and estimated at 0.15%. In this case, analysis on RBCs proved invaluable, as it confirmed the presence of a PNH clone with a size of 0.04% ( the figures indicated were obtained using the FACSCanto II cytometer, see Figure , upper panels). Another virtual case highlighted the interest of the PNH clone size quantification on RBCs. It involved a 30‐year‐old man diagnosed with classical PNH, presenting a major PNH clone at 93.12% on neutrophils and 94.2% on monocytes, and 33.00% on RBCs at diagnosis. The files sent to the participants corresponded to the 1‐year follow‐up during eculizumab treatment [ ]. The clone size slightly increased on WBCs (96.99% on neutrophils and 95.9% on monocytes; the figures indicated were obtained using the FACSCanto II cytometer, see Figure , upper panels). An expected increase in size to 92.56% was observed in RBCs, indicating successful therapy, as eculizumab prevents hemolysis of the GPI‐deficient PNH RBCs [ ]. Among the 20 surveys, we challenged the participants with the case of a 57‐year‐old woman with aplastic anemia who underwent bone marrow transplantation. The PNH clone, initially estimated at 1.40% on neutrophils, 7.1% on monocytes, and 0.36% on RBCs at diagnosis ( the figures indicated were obtained using the Navios cytometer, see Figure , lower panels), disappeared in the follow‐up sample (Figure ). 3.4 Improving Practices in <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">PNH</styled-content> Diagnosis Since reporting is a crucial part of the process, we created a compact guide designed to fit in a laboratory coat pocket, aimed at harmonizing PNH test conclusions in accordance with the successive international recommendations [ , , , , ]. We analyzed the conformity of the final reports provided by the participants in cases of both PNH clone presence (Figure ) and absence (Figure ). Over the past 10 years, we have proudly observed a significant increase in conformity for both clinical situations, reaching 96%. 3.5 Towards the Next Workshop Dedicated to <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">RBC</styled-content> Assay The initial workshop we conducted played a crucial role in the harmonization of PNH testing in France. While we focused on implementing WBC analysis for PNH testing, there is now a pressing need to improve the RBC assay. We are planning to organize a dedicated workshop in 2025 to present the newly developed screening test involving immature RBCs (iRBCs) [ ]. Indeed, the PNH clone size evaluated in CD71+ RBCs appears to be larger than in mature RBCs and correlates with that in both neutrophils and monocytes [ ]. The major advantage of the CD71 addition is the more reliable separation between true PNH type II and PNH type III cells versus the incorrect inclusion of transfused cells into the PNH RBC clone. The reason for the almost identical PNH clone size between the lineages is that the iRBCs are not prone to complement‐mediated lysis. Moreover, detection of C3d deposit on RBCs by flow cytometry in anti‐C5‐treated patients may be of interest for assessing extravascular hemolysis [ ]. 4 A Strong Network of Cytometrists Built in France Following the diagnostic practice harmonization spread in France since 2013 through our ongoing inter‐laboratory comparison program, our PNH working group initiated a nationwide multicenter prospective observational study on February 29, 2016, in order to collect all PNH cases or GPI‐deficient cells above 0.01%. The first main objective is to monitor the long‐term evolution of minor PNH clones < 1%, which represent over one third of positive samples [ ], using high‐resolution flow cytometry, as previous evaluations showed the disappearance of PNH clones in 6%–24% of patients with bone marrow failure over 3–5 years with a 2‐color flow cytometry procedure [ , ]. The second objective aims to further investigate the relevance of classifying type II and type III PNH cells in WBCs in clones larger than 1%, as the significance of this distinction—unlike in RBCs—remains unclear. The collected data at diagnosis and during long‐term follow‐up are currently under analysis. This experience and the strong network of cytometrists we have built since the workshop conducted in 2010 led us to create in 2018 the French‐speaking flow cytometry association in Hematology, namely the CytHem for Cytometry in Hematology ( https://www.cythem.fr ). Its main purpose is to harmonize the diagnostic practices by sharing technical protocols and gating strategies for the different instruments equipping the routine laboratories. Eleven working groups have been created, each dedicated to a specific hemopathy or disease group (PNH, chronic myelomonocytic leukemia, myelodysplastic neoplasms, acute myeloid leukemia, mature B‐cell neoplasms, central nervous lymphomas, granular lymphocytic leukemia, lymphoblastic leukemia, Sezary Syndrome, plasma cell neoplasms), except CytHem‐questions, which was established to address practical issues, provide information, and manage In Vitro Diagnosis Regulations (IVDR) concerns. Each disease working group is closely related to a French‐speaking clinical association. The PNH working group is indeed working alongside the rare immuno‐hematological diseases (MaRIH) healthcare network ( https://marih.fr ). chunks.content: Introduction Overactive bladder (OAB) represents one of the most prevalent and clinically significant pediatric urological conditions, affecting approximately 5–12% of children aged 5–10 years worldwide [ ]. According to the International Children’s Continence Society, pediatric OAB is defined as urinary urgency, typically with frequency and nocturia, with or without urinary incontinence, occurring without urinary tract infection or other obvious pathology [ ]. Pediatric OAB presents as a complex set of urinary symptoms that impact children and families [ ]. Symptoms include increased daytime frequency, an urgent need to urinate with holding maneuvers, daytime accidents, and nocturnal enuresis [ ]. In addition to physical symptoms, it also leads to psychosocial consequences, as children often face social embarrassment and isolation, withdraw from peer activities, and experience a lower quality of life that impacts both their development and family dynamics [ ]. The management of pediatric OAB follows a stepwise approach, starting with conservative measures such as behavioral interventions and lifestyle modifications before pharmacological interventions [ ]. When non-pharmacological methods fail, antimuscarinic agents are the primary medical treatment [ ]. Despite their efficacy, they are limited by anticholinergic side effects such as dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, and headache [ ]. Mirabegron stimulates β3 receptors in the detrusor muscle, inducing relaxation during storage, which improves bladder capacity and decreases contractility [ ]. In contrast to antimuscarinics, it maintains normal voiding function and reduces residual urine [ ]. A comprehensive pooled analysis of three large phase III studies revealed that mirabegron significantly improved incontinence and micturition, with efficacy comparable to that of antimuscarinics and superior tolerability in adults with OAB [ ]. Mirabegron has been shown in multiple trials to be effective in treating OAB in adults and was adopted by the NICE guidelines in 2013 [ – ]. As a β3 agonist, it also appears safe and effective in children with OAB, improving urodynamic parameters and clinical symptoms, and provides an alternative for refractory or antimuscarinic-intolerant patients [ , ]. Previous studies comparing mirabegron and solifenacin in paediatric OAB patients have shown varying results. Soliman et al. reported that both agents are effective, with mirabegron showing better tolerability [ ]. Kim et al. reported similar efficacy and safety, whereas Mansour et al. suggested that mirabegron may offer superior outcomes with fewer adverse effects [ , ]. However, no systematic review has compared these agents in children. Therefore, this review aimed to evaluate evidence comparing the efficacy and safety of mirabegron versus solifenacin in children with OAB, aiming to offer insights that can guide clinical decisions and optimize treatment. Methods Protocol This systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted and reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines [ ]. The study protocol was registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) under the registration number CRD420251129236. Search strategy A comprehensive literature search was conducted across four electronic databases: PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library, up to September 2, 2025. No date restrictions were applied; however, the search was limited to studies published in English. The search strategy combined keywords and medical subject headings related to the pediatric population, overactive bladder, mirabegron, and solifenacin. The detailed search strategy for databases is provided in Appendix 1. Eligibility criteria Studies eligible for this review included randomized controlled trials, clinical trials, prospective or retrospective cohort studies, and case‒control studies that directly compared mirabegron and solifenacin as monotherapies. The study population was children and adolescents (≤ 18 years) diagnosed with non-neurogenic OAB. Conversely, studies were excluded if they were case reports, case series, reviews, or editorials. Additionally, studies without a direct comparator arm or those focusing exclusively on neurogenic bladder populations were not included. Outcome definition The efficacy outcome was treatment response, although its definition varied across the included studies. Mansour et al. defined efficacy as a ≥ 50% reduction in the baseline Dysfunctional Voiding Scoring System (DVSS) score [ ]. Soliman et al. used a similar threshold, defining success as a > 50% improvement based on a symptom relief questionnaire [ ] In contrast, Kim et al. defined a response as a ≥ 90% reduction in symptoms based on patient and parent reports [ ]. The safety outcome was assessed as the occurrence of any treatment-related adverse events. Study selection Studies imported into the Rayyan web application for systematic reviews [ ]. After duplicate records were manually removed, two reviewers independently and blindly screened the titles and abstracts of the remaining articles to assess their relevance. The full texts of the studies that met our predetermined inclusion criteria were subsequently screened. After duplicate records were manually removed, two reviewers independently and blindly screened the titles and abstracts of the remaining articles to assess their relevance. The full texts of the studies that met our predetermined inclusion criteria were subsequently screened. Any disagreements during the selection process were resolved by discussion and agreement with a third reviewer. The flow diagram was generated via the PRISMA2020 R package and Shiny app [ ]. Quality assessment and publication bias The quality of the included studies was independently assessed by two blinded reviewers, with any disagreements resolved by a third reviewer. Randomized controlled trials were evaluated with the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool 2 (RoB 2) [ ] which covers seven domains: random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding of participants and investigators, blinding of outcome assessors, incomplete outcome data, selective reporting, and other potential biases. Each domain is rated as “low risk,” “high risk,” or “some concerns.” Non-randomized studies, including cohort designs, were assessed using the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale (NOS) [ ]. Three areas are evaluated: selection of study groups (up to four stars), comparability of groups (up to two stars), and ascertainment of exposure or outcome (up to three stars). Based on total scores, studies were categorized as high, moderate, or low quality, with higher scores indicating better methodological rigor. Statistical analysis Dichotomous outcomes (treatment response and the incidence of adverse events) were analyzed using the Risk Ratio (RR) with its 95% confidence interval (CI) to estimate effects. Due to the expected clinical and methodological heterogeneity among the included studies, a random-effects model was employed for meta-analysis. Statistical heterogeneity was measured with Higgins’ I² test. According to established guidelines, an I² value of 0–40% indicates insignificant heterogeneity, 30–60% suggests moderate heterogeneity, 50–90% reflects substantial heterogeneity, and 75–100% shows considerable heterogeneity [ ]. To test the robustness of the results and determine the influence of each study on the overall estimate, a sensitivity analysis was performed by removing one study at a time and reanalyzing the data. All statistical analyses for this review were conducted using Review Manager software Version 5.3 [ ]. Results Study selection As shown in Fig. , our search strategy yielded a total of 222 studies from four databases. After eliminating 55 duplicate records, 167 studies remained for screening. Of these, 162 were excluded based on title and abstract screening. After full-text screening, three studies were included in the review, involving a total of 246 patients, with 116 patients treated with mirabegron and 130 patients treated with solifenacin. Baseline characteristics The total sample size across the included studies was 116 patients in the mirabegron group and 130 patients in the solifenacin group. The mean age (SD) was 9.44 years (1.97) for the Mirabegron group and 8.55 years (2.21) for the Solifenacin group, with an overall range of 5–15 years across included studies. Overall, 41.8% of the participants were male. The Mansour and Soliman studies followed both treatment groups for 12 weeks, whereas Kim et al. followed Mirabegron patients for 34 weeks and Solifenacin patients for 28 weeks. The baseline characteristics of the included studies are shown in Table . Clinical characteristics and outcomes Table outlined the characteristics and clinical outcomes of pediatric patients with OAB treated with mirabegron versus solifenacin across three studies: Kim et al., Mansour et al., and Soliman et al. Mansour et al. and Soliman et al. were single-blind randomized controlled trials (RCTs), whereas Kim et al. was an observational study. All studies included pediatric patients with idiopathic non-neurogenic OAB aged from 5 to 15 years. The intervention consisted of a daily single dose of mirabegron at 50 mg, with weight-adjusted dosing in Mansour et al., whereas the comparator was a daily single dose of solifenacin at 5 mg across all studies. Fewer adverse events were consistently associated with mirabegron than with solifenacin. The efficacy outcomes showed that Mirabegron was comparable to solifenacin in Kim et al. and Soliman et al., whereas Mansour et al. reported greater efficacy for Mirabegron. Risk-of-bias assessment and publication bias The observational study by Kim et al., evaluated with the NOS, scored 7 out of 9 stars, indicating good overall quality. It received the maximum score for selection, one star for comparability, and two stars for outcome assessment. Among the randomized controlled trials, Mansour et al. demonstrated a low overall risk of bias across all domains, with no concerns regarding randomization, deviations from intervention, missing outcome data, outcome measurement, or selective reporting. In contrast, Soliman et al. was judged to have a high overall risk of bias, primarily due to issues with the randomization process, deviations from the intended intervention, and selective reporting of outcomes, while outcome measurement and data completeness were considered low risk. Efficacy outcomes The pooled analysis of all three studies indicated that mirabegron was not statistically superior to solifenacin in achieving treatment response (RR = 1.11, 95% CI: 0.92–1.33, p = 0.28). Notably, substantial heterogeneity was observed across studies (I² = 58%, p = 0.09), arising from differing treatment-response definitions. However, Explanatory sensitivity was done by excluding the study by Soliman et al. (assessed as high risk of bias), the pooled estimate from the remaining two studies demonstrated a statistically significant benefit of mirabegron over solifenacin (RR = 1.24, 95% CI: 1.04–1.47, p = 0.02), and in this sensitivity analysis heterogeneity was fully resolved (I² = 0%) Fig. . Safety outcome As shown in Fig. , mirabegron was associated with a 56% lower risk of adverse events than solifenacin. The incidence of adverse events was 16.4% (19/116) for mirabegron and 35.4% (46/130) for solifenacin. The pooled risk ratio was 0.44 (95% CI 0.28–0.70; Z = 3.52, p = 0.0004), with negligible heterogeneity (I² = 0%). All three studies favoured mirabegron, with Soliman et al. and Mansour et al. contributing the most to the pooled effect. Discussion This systematic review and meta-analysis summarized current evidence comparing the efficacy and safety of mirabegron and solifenacin in children with non-neurogenic OAB. Across three studies involving 246 patients, pooled analysis suggested no difference in treatment response. However, after excluding the high-risk study, the sensitivity analysis suggested that mirabegron had superior efficacy. This finding is based on only two studies with a combined sample size of 117 patients and should be interpreted cautiously as hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory. Notably, mirabegron demonstrated a 56% lower risk of treatment-related adverse events, indicating a better short-term safety profile. The studies included children ranging from 5 to 15 years of age (mean age 6–10 years), which is typical for pediatric OAB populations [ ]. At baseline, symptom burden was similar across groups, with common OAB features such as urgency, frequency, daytime incontinence, and nocturnal enuresis [ , , ]. Differences in study design may explain variations in reported efficacy. For example, Kim et al. defined response as ≥ 90% symptom improvement, while Mansour and Soliman defined response as ≥ 50% symptom improvement [ – ]. This variability highlights the need for standardized outcome measures in future pediatric OAB research. Our results showed that mirabegron might be effective as solifenacin in children with OAB, which is consistent with findings in adults. Wang et al. reported no significant differences between mirabegron 50 mg and solifenacin 5 mg in reducing incontinence, urgency, or micturition frequency [ ]. These results align with those of a trial conducted by Batista et al. and studies by Jamil et al. and Scaldazza et al., which reported comparable symptom relief [ – ]. Likewise, Soliman et al. and Kim et al. found no superiority of either drug in pediatric populations [ , ]. Conversely, Mansour et al. reported higher response rates with mirabegron [ ]. Solifenacin blocks M3 muscarinic receptors, while mirabegron stimulates β3-adrenergic receptors, but both drugs lead to detrusor muscle relaxation during bladder storage [ , , ]. This shared physiological effect may explain their comparable efficacy in reducing urgency, frequency, and incontinence. However, variations in results across studies likely arise from differences in patient populations, baseline symptom severity, prior treatment exposure, and the tools used for symptom evaluation. However, given the limited number of included studies and small sample sizes, these findings should be considered preliminary. In terms of safety, our analysis suggested that mirabegron was associated with a significantly lower incidence of adverse events than solifenacin in children, with overall event rates of 16.4% versus 35.4%, representing a relative reduction of approximately 56%. Adverse events associated with solifenacin were most commonly constipation, dry mouth, and headache, whereas mirabegron was associated with fewer and generally milder effects, such as headache or transient gastrointestinal discomfort. These results are consistent with previous studies in adults, where anticholinergic agents like solifenacin are consistently linked to constipation and dry mouth, while mirabegron demonstrates a more favourable safety profile [ – ]. This difference is likely due to their pharmacological mechanisms, as solifenacin has anticholinergic effects that affect multiple organs, whereas mirabegron acts as a β3-adrenergic receptor agonist, selectively targeting detrusor smooth muscle with limited systemic spillover or off-target effects that are common with solifenacin [ , ]. The better tolerability of mirabegron is important in pediatrics, where side effects often cause treatment discontinuation [ ]. By lowering this risk, mirabegron may support adherence and symptom control, potentially offering a safer short-term option for treating OAB in children within the limitations of current evidence. Our findings related to non-neurogenic (idiopathic) OAB, for which neither mirabegron nor solifenacin has pediatric approval. Mirabegron received FDA approval in 2021 for neurogenic detrusor overactivity (NDO) in children ≥ 3 years, but remains off-label for idiopathic pediatric OAB [ ]. Similarly, solifenacin has pediatric approval only for NDO [ ]. Nevertheless, both agents are commonly prescribed in practice, highlighting the need for systematic evidence synthesis to guide decision-making without formal regulatory guidance. Current treatments and future perspectives Antimuscarinic agents are the primary treatment for pediatric OAB, with oxybutynin and tolterodine being the only approved medications [ ]. However, their limited uroselectivity and associated adverse effects contribute to poor treatment persistence (11.8%) and high discontinuation rates (32%) [ , ]. Concerns have also been raised regarding neurodevelopmental safety, particularly because oxybutynin crosses the blood–brain barrier. Nonetheless, current evidence has not demonstrated measurable cognitive harm [ , ]. However, long-term neurodevelopmental data remain limited. Considering these limitations, β3-adrenoceptor agonists have emerged as alternative therapies [ ]. Despite their therapeutic potential, cardiovascular safety remains a key concern, as Chapple et al. reported increases in heart rate and blood pressure, necessitating regular monitoring [ ]. To optimize efficacy while mitigating dose-related adverse effects, dual therapy has been explored. In pediatric overactive bladder, this approach combines an antimuscarinic, typically solifenacin, with the β3-agonist mirabegron to enhance bladder relaxation through complementary mechanisms [ ]. In adults, combination therapy has demonstrated greater efficacy than monotherapy [ – ]. Similarly, in children refractory to antimuscarinics, add-on mirabegron improved bladder capacity and continence with generally mild side effects [ , ]. Overall, dual therapy appears promising and well-tolerated; however, randomized pediatric trials are still needed. Beyond established therapies, Vibegron is a highly selective β3-adrenoceptor agonist with a potentially more favorable cardiovascular profile than mirabegron [ ]. A comprehensive adult review confirmed vibegron’s high β3-AR selectivity, effective symptom relief, minimal cardiovascular effects, and favorable tolerability that may support better long-term adherence [ ]. Kato et al. reported the first pediatric case of vibegron use for anticholinergic-resistant neurogenic detrusor overactivity, demonstrating improved bladder compliance and resolution of detrusor overactivity on urodynamic assessment [ ]. Subsequently, Kitta et al. provided the first urodynamic evaluation of vibegron in children and adolescents with idiopathic OAB, documenting improvements in both subjective symptoms and lower urinary tract function [ ]. These findings suggest that vibegron may be a promising option for children refractory to anticholinergics, although larger prospective studies are required to confirm its safety and long-term efficacy. In parallel with pharmacologic therapies, high-dose vitamin D supplementation (VDS) has been explored as a safe and accessible strategy for pediatric OAB. In a three-arm randomized clinical trial, Chen et al. demonstrated that high-dose VDS (2400 IU/day) combined with standard urotherapy resulted in greater improvements in voiding frequency compared with solifenacin plus urotherapy or urotherapy alone, with an excellent safety profile [ ]. A secondary analysis indicated that the therapeutic effect was more pronounced in children with baseline vitamin D levels of 20–35 ng/mL and more severe symptoms [ ].Vitamin D deficiency was also more prevalent in children with OAB-related urinary incontinence than in healthy controls, and supplementation was shown to reduce urinary symptoms and improve quality of life in treatment-resistant cases [ ]. These findings suggest that vitamin D may influence bladder function and that baseline vitamin D status could modify treatment response; however, larger studies are needed to confirm mechanisms, optimal dosing, and long-term outcomes. When pharmacological therapy is ineffective or poorly tolerated, third-line therapies like intradetrusor botulinum toxin A (BoNT-A) injections and percutaneous tibial nerve stimulation (PTNS) are considered, though their pediatric use is limited by practical constraints [ – ]. BoNT-A is FDA-approved for pediatric neurogenic detrusor overactivity and benefits refractory OAB, with response rates of around 50% [ – ]. However, its effects last only 6–9 months, requiring repeat injections under anesthesia, increasing cost risks, procedure complications, and family burden [ ]. PTNS has shown efficacy, with improved durability versus antimuscarinic therapy alone, but requires weekly 30-minute office sessions plus maintenance therapy, while pediatric in-home protocols remain unstudied [ , ]. Although clinically effective, the requirement for repeated in-office treatments may limit accessibility and long-term adherence in children, highlighting the need for validated home-based neuromodulation strategies. For this reason, focus has shifted toward noninvasive neuromodulation strategies. A systematic review and meta-analysis of eight randomized trials found that parasacral transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) produced 3.34-fold higher complete response rates than standard therapy, without significant adverse effects [ ] Lin et al. reported that transcutaneous pelvic floor magnetic stimulation combined with voiding training achieved superior outcomes compared with voiding training alone in children with OAB [ ]. Sacral neuromodulation (SNM) is being explored in refractory pediatric cases. Although sacral neuromodulation is not FDA-approved for children under 16 years for urological indications, off-label pediatric studies have demonstrated overall symptom improvement in approximately 68% of patients and complete resolution in 39%, with concurrent improvements in quality of life and urodynamic findings; however, these benefits must be weighed against notable complication and reoperation rates [ ]. SNM may be considered a viable third-line option in carefully selected pediatric patients, while emphasizing the need for standardized protocols and larger multicenter studies to define long-term efficacy. The findings of this meta-analysis should be considered preliminary due to several key limitations. Only three studies met the inclusion criteria, and with relatively small sample sizes, which limits the statistical power and generalizability of our findings. The substantial variability among the included studies in terms of design, follow-up duration, and definitions of treatment response constitutes a major methodological limitation. This inconsistency not only undermines confidence in the pooled efficacy estimate but also likely contributed significantly to the observed heterogeneity. Importantly, the safety conclusions of this meta-analysis are limited to short-term adverse events observed during follow-up periods of 12–34 weeks. Therefore, the long-term safety of mirabegron and solifenacin in the pediatric population cannot be determined based on the currently available evidence. Furthermore, none of the studies evaluated cognitive outcomes, which is an important factor when comparing antimuscarinic and non-antimuscarinic therapies in children [ ]. Finally, because the included studies enrolled children aged 5–15 years, the findings may not be generalizable to infants, toddlers, or older adolescents. Despite these limitations, our study is the first meta-analysis to compare mirabegron and solifenacin in the treatment of pediatric OAB directly. The results suggest that mirabegron may be an effective and safer alternative; however, further high-quality, randomized controlled trials with standardized outcome definitions and longer follow-up periods are needed. Conclusions This systematic review and meta-analysis summarized evidence comparing mirabegron and solifenacin in pediatric OAB. The pooled data suggested comparable efficacy, with mirabegron showing a favorable short-term adverse event profile. However, given the few included studies and limited sample size, these findings are preliminary. Larger, multicenter RCTs with standardized outcomes and longer follow-up are needed to confirm these observations and inform clinical decisions. Supplementary Information Supplementary Material 1. chunks.content: Introduction Nocturnal enuresis (NE) is a prevalent condition among children characterized by involuntary urination during sleep [ , ]. Cross-national studies reveal significant regional variations in the prevalence of NE among children: European children aged 5–15 years show the highest prevalence at 12% [ – ], while India reports 11.89% among school-aged children (6–15 years) [ ]. The prevalence of NE in 5-year-old children in China is 15.13% and shows a decreasing trend with age [ , ]. Notably, Saudi Arabia exhibits the highest prevalence at 24% [ ]. The occurrence of NE is associated with various factors, including genetic, physiological, and psychological influences. Research has shown that children are at an increased risk of developing NE if their parents have a history of the condition [ ]. Furthermore, gender is a factor, with boys being more likely than girls to experience NE [ ]. In addition, it is reported that NE not only leads to varying degrees of psychosocial stress and diminished self-esteem in affected children but also contributes to anxiety among their parents or caregivers [ ]. Therefore, continued research into the early detection and intervention of NE is of vital importance for the future of our children populations. Sleep-disordered breathing (SDB) in children and adolescents refers to a spectrum of breathing disorders occurring during sleep, ranging from primary snoring to obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) [ ]. The most severe manifestation of SDB is obstructive OSA, characterized by recurrent partial or complete upper airway obstruction during sleep, resulting in abnormal ventilation and disrupted sleep patterns [ ]. The prevalence of sleep disorders in childhood is at least 25%-50%, with a peak incidence between the ages of 3 and 8 years [ , ]. The prevalence of pediatric OSA ranges from 1.2% to 5.7% [ ], and it is increasing alongside the rising trends of childhood obesity [ ]. These children typically exhibit adverse reactions, including attention deficits, behavioral and emotional issues, morning headaches, excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS), and growth retardation [ ]. According to the International Classification of Sleep Disorders, Third Edition, the diagnosis of pediatric OSA is based on clinical history, an apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) ≥ 1, and findings from polysomnography (PSG), which remains the gold standard for diagnosing OSA in children and adolescents [ , ]. Although there are many risk factors for NE, the relationship between NE and SDB remains ambiguous and debated in the existing literature. Both conditions are prevalent in pediatric populations and are associated with substantial long-term health consequences [ ]. Studies have shown that the prevalence of NE in children and adolescents aged 6–11 with OSA is 4.6%, with no significant difference between children without OSA [ ]. However, some studies have suggested mild SDB is not significantly correlated with NE, while severe OSA may significantly increase the risk [ ]. Different studies’ results are inconsistent, indicating the need for further research to elucidate this association. Although some studies have suggested an independent correlation between NE and severe SDB, such as OSA, there is still a lack of research focusing on the occurrence and relationship between NE and varying degrees of SDB. Therefore, this meta-analysis aimed to investigate the prevalence of SDB in participants with NE (SWN) and the prevalence of NE in participants with SDB (NWS) based on the available data and to determine the association between NE and different severities of SDB in 5–18 children. Methods Study selection and selection criteria This study followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses 2020 (PRISMA 2020) guidelines and was registered in PROSPERO (registration number: CRD42024576610). A systematic search was conducted in four electronic databases: PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, and Cochrane. The search included the keywords ‘Nocturnal Enuresis’ and ‘Sleep Apnea, Obstructive’ from database inception to 17 May 2024. Inclusion criteria required case-control, cohort, or cross-sectional studies involving populations with clearly defined diagnostic criteria for NE and/or OSA. Studies were excluded if they did not report or allow calculation of NE or OSA cases, lacked extractable data, or were literature reviews, case reports, animal studies, conference abstracts, or non-English publications. Data extraction Based on the inclusion and exclusion criteria, two reviewers (YKL and SDS) independently assessed the eligibility of the studies, with final decisions made in consultation with an arbitrator (GWS). Data were extracted following standardized procedures, including details such as the first author, publication date, country, study design, sample source, sample size, mean age, gender ratio, methods used to assess NE and SDB (measurement techniques, diagnostic criteria, and thresholds), and all relevant covariates modifying the relationship between NE and SDB. The study’s primary outcomes were the pooled prevalence of NE and SDB, as well as the crude and adjusted effect estimates of the association between NE and SDB, expressed as ORs with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Classification and diagnostic criteria for NE and SDB In this study, the study population comprises children and adolescents aged 5–18 years, and the term children and adolescents is used consistently throughout the manuscript to reflect this age range. Children and adolescents aged 5–18 years were included in this study. The diagnosis of NE in children and adolescents was primarily based on the International Children’s Continence Society (ICCS) criteria (used in 12 studies): urinary incontinence occurring ≥ 1 time/month for ≥ 3 months in children and adolescents aged ≥ 5 years, excluding organic causes. Other diagnostic criteria included: the Pediatric Sleep Questionnaire (PSQ-22) in one study, the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fourth Edition, Text Revision (DSM IV-TR) in one study, the International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision (ICD-10) in one study, and the International Classification of Diseases, 9th Revision, Clinical Modification (ICD-9-CM) in one study. Additionally, one study used a non-validated questionnaire. Two studies defined enuresis by frequency: one as ≥ 5 times per month (type unknown) and another as ≥ 3 times per week (type unknown). The cases of NE collected in this study were predominantly monosymptomatic enuresis (PMNE/MNE), and some studies did not distinguish subtypes. SDB was diagnosed primarily by PSG in 12 studies. Obstructive sleep apnea-hypopnea syndrome (OSAHS) was diagnosed based on the apnea-hypopnea index (AHI). In children and adolescents, OSAHS is typically defined as an AHI ≥ 1 event per hour, differing from adult criteria. The severity of OSAHS was categorized as mild (AHI 1–5 events/hour), moderate (AHI > 5–10 events/hour), and severe (AHI > 10 events/hour). However, specific AHI thresholds varied: two studies used the respiratory disturbance index (RDI) ≥ 1 event/hour. Additionally, three studies used the modified Pediatric Sleep Questionnaire (PSQ-22), one study used the International Classification of Diseases (ICD-9-CM) criteria, and three studies diagnosed SDB based on frequent snoring (≥ 3 times per week) reported in questionnaires. One study used adenoid-nasopharyngeal ratio (ANR) ≥ 0.5, and another used both snoring questionnaire and ANR. Two studies employed the OSA-18 and PSQ-22 questionnaires. Research quality assessment The quality of each study was independently assessed by two researchers (YKL and SDS) using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) for cohort and case-control studies, and the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ) scale for cross-sectional studies. The maximum score for cohort studies was 9, while for cross-sectional studies it was 11. Higher scores indicated better methodological quality, with studies scoring > 5 on NOS or > 8 on AHRQ considered of moderate to high reliability (Appendix S2). Any discrepancies were resolved through consultation with Guowei Si to reach a final decision. Statistical analyses This meta-analysis applied a random-effects model to obtain relatively conservative findings when significant heterogeneity was detected (I² > 50%, P < 0.05) based on the I² test. A fixed-effects model was used if no significant heterogeneity was observed (I² < 50%). Subgroup analyses were conducted to identify potential sources of heterogeneity. The quality and robustness of the results were assessed through sensitivity analyses. Additionally, publication bias was evaluated using funnel plots and Egger’s test. All data analyses were performed using Stata version 15.1 (StataCorp LLC, TX, USA, http://www.stata.com ). The initially conducted database search identified 784 articles. After removing duplicates and screening titles and abstracts based on inclusion and exclusion criteria, 469 articles were included. A full-text review of 53 articles resulted in the exclusion of 19 articles, leaving 34 articles for further assessment. Finally, 22 studies were included in the meta-analysis. Similarly, Egger’s test showed P = 0.261 ( P > 0.05) for the prevalence of NWS, confirming the absence of significant publication bias. Sensitivity analysis further demonstrated the robustness of the results. Table Presents the results of the subgroup analysis for the prevalence of SWN. The analysis showed that diagnostic criteria and assessment methods significantly influenced prevalence estimates. For studies diagnosing NE according to ICCS guidelines, the pooled prevalence was 48.7% (95% CI: 0.283–0.691), whereas those using ICD-9-CM reported only 1.6% (95% CI: 0.011–0.021). Similarly, differences were observed in SDB assessment methods. Studies using PSG and PSQ-22 yielded comparable prevalence estimates (51.2% and 52.8%, respectively), while studies applying ICD-9-CM criteria again showed much lower prevalence (1.6%). By study design, cross-sectional studies reported a higher pooled prevalence (41.6%) than case-control studies (13.6%). The study setting (community vs. hospital) did not substantially affect prevalence estimates. Sample size appeared to influence SWN prevalence: studies with small sample sizes (≤ 60) reported higher prevalence (61.3%), while very large studies (≥ 1000) showed markedly lower estimates (1.6%), suggesting a possible sample size effect. Regional differences were evident. The pooled prevalence was 2.0% in Asia, 32.9% in Europe, 52.8% in Africa, and 62.0% in America, indicating substantial variation across regions. Gender composition also appeared to affect prevalence. Studies with a female majority reported higher prevalence (49.0%) than those with a male majority (22.6%). One study with an unclear gender distribution showed a higher rate, but this result should be interpreted cautiously due to the single-study limitation. Overall, these findings suggest that methodological differences, regional factors, and gender composition contribute to the heterogeneity observed in the reported prevalence of SWN. Subgroup analyses further demonstrated that both mild SDB (primary snoring) and moderate-to-severe SDB (obstructive sleep apnea, OSA) were associated with an increased risk of NE, with comparable effect sizes. Although no clear dose-response relationship across SDB severity levels was identified, it is noteworthy that the point estimates numerically suggested a higher risk associated with moderate-to-severe SDB compared with mild SDB. This difference, however, did not reach statistical significance, which may reflect limited statistical power and heterogeneity across studies rather than a true absence of a biological gradient. In addition to hormonal factors, sex-specific differences in neuroendocrine regulation, including central arousal pathways and autonomic nervous system control, may also play an important role in modulating the interaction between sleep-disordered breathing and bladder function. However, these mechanisms remain insufficiently explored and warrant further investigation. Evidence from diverse countries further supports the global relevance of SDB–NE comorbidity. Studies from Italy, Saudi Arabia, Indonesia, Australia, Greece, and the United States consistently report higher rates of sleep-disordered breathing symptoms among children and adolescents with NE, as well as an increased prevalence of NE among those with SDB [ ]. Collectively, these findings underscore that the coexistence of NE and SDB is not restricted to specific cultural or geographic settings. Several studies have also identified obesity and upper airway abnormalities as important shared risk factors for NE and SDB. Chinese and Egyptian cohorts have reported that obesity, tonsillar hypertrophy, and elevated adenoid-to-nasopharyngeal ratios are associated with higher risks of both conditions [ ]. In addition, elevated plasma brain natriuretic peptide levels in children with comorbid NE and SDB suggest that cardiovascular and hemodynamic factors may contribute to the underlying pathophysiology [ ]. Together, these findings indicate that multiple interacting mechanisms, ranging from anatomical obstruction to sleep fragmentation and neurohumoral changes may underlie the observed association. Our meta-analysis also provides evidence that mild SDB, including habitual snoring, is not a benign condition in the context of NE. Although some individual studies have reported no significant association between isolated snoring and NE [ ], the pooled estimates from our analysis suggest that even mild SDB is linked to a higher risk of NE. This discrepancy may reflect differences in sample size and diagnostic criteria across studies. While the exact mechanisms remain to be clarified, subtle alterations in sleep architecture and arousal thresholds associated with mild SDB may play a role in impairing nocturnal bladder control. Several limitations of this study should be acknowledged. First, substantial heterogeneity existed across included studies with respect to design, diagnostic criteria, and population characteristics, which may have influenced the pooled estimates. Second, only English-language publications were included, potentially introducing language bias. Third, most of the available evidence was derived from cross-sectional and case-control studies, limiting causal inference. Moreover, variations in parental reporting of NE may have contributed to misclassification bias. Although sensitivity analyses did not materially alter the main findings, future well-designed longitudinal studies are needed to better elucidate the temporal relationship between SDB and NE. Conclusion A significant association exists between SDB and NE, with a high prevalence of both SDB among individuals with NE and NE among those with SDB. Both mild SDB (such as primary snoring) and moderate-to-severe SDB (e.g., obstructive sleep apnea) are associated with an increased risk of NE. Although no clear gradient in risk across different SDB severity levels was observed, these findings suggest that even mild forms of SDB deserve clinical attention. Early identification and management of SDB may represent a promising strategy for the prevention of NE. Further well-designed studies are warranted to clarify severity-specific effects and to determine whether treatment of mild SDB can effectively reduce the incidence of NE. chunks.content: Introduction Bladder and bowel dysfunction (BBD) is defined by the coexistence of functional constipation and lower urinary tract symptoms, including urgency, altered voiding frequency, daytime urinary incontinence (DUI), and nocturnal enuresis in children 5 years or older. , BBD is common yet frequently underdiagnosed, affecting up to 20% of 7-year-olds , and accounting for approximately 40% of pediatric urology referrals. BBD increases the risk of upper urinary tract infections, , , , kidney scarring, chronic kidney disease, and hypertension , and adversely affects self-esteem and quality of life. , Anatomical and neurophysiologic interactions between the bladder and bowel contribute to symptom overlap. , Consequently, current treatment strategies adopt a stepwise approach, prioritizing bowel management before lower urinary tract symptom–specific interventions. , Bowel management includes education, disimpaction, maintenance therapy, and scheduled toileting after meals. Lower urinary tract symptom–specific therapy includes standard urotherapy (SU), emphasizing timed voiding every 2 to 3 hours, optimal posture, discouragement of holding behaviors, and adequate fluid intake. , , When initial interventions are insufficient, the International Children’s Continence Society (ICCS) recommends targeted urotherapy, such as pelvic floor retraining, biofeedback, neuromodulation, and intermittent catheterization, or pharmacologic treatment, typically beginning with anticholinergics. , The initial stepwise treatment approach is supported by limited evidence, with only a few studies suggesting that bowel management alone may reduce DUI in affected children. , Current recommendations regarding sequencing of treatment modalities, including those endorsed by the European Association of Urology and the European Society of Paediatric Urology, supported by the ICCS are based on low-level evidence. , Thus, high-quality prospective data to guide the optimal order of therapeutic components for children with BBD are highly warranted. This randomized clinical trial (RCT) aimed to evaluate whether combining SU with bowel management improves DUI compared with bowel management alone in children with BBD. Methods Study Design and Participants This multicenter, open-label, parallel-group RCT enrolled children aged 5 to 14 years with treatment-naive BBD from 5 hospital outpatient clinics across Denmark (Aarhus, Aalborg, Gødstrup, Viborg, and Kolding) via primary care referrals and social media from September 1, 2022, to July 31, 2025, with 12-week follow-up. Eligibility required functional constipation (≥2 Rome IV criteria) and DUI at least twice weekly for 1 month or longer. Exclusion criteria included known anatomical or neurologic urinary or gastrointestinal abnormalities, prior or current urotherapy, or pharmacologic DUI treatment. Children receiving laxative monotherapy were eligible if constipation remained uncontrolled. Full criteria are in eTable 1 in . The trial was planned according to SPIRIT 2013 guidelines and is reported per the Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials ( CONSORT ) reporting guidelines. The full trial protocol and statistical analysis plan are available in . The study was approved by the Regional Committee on Health Research Ethics of the Central Denmark Region and registered at ClinicalTrials.gov. Written informed consent was obtained from the parents or legal guardians before enrollment. Randomization and Masking Participants were block-randomized 1:1 within each study site using variable block sizes , , , , , , via the electronic REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture) portal, which automatically concealed the allocation sequence. , Study personnel who enrolled participants did not have access to future allocations. Due to the behavioral nature of SU, participants and caregivers were not blinded. Outcome assessors and data analysts were aware of group assignments. Intervention Participants received 12 weeks of individually tailored bowel management according to the European Society for Paediatric Gastroenterology, Hepatology, and Nutrition guidelines, alone or combined with SU. Bowel management included disimpaction with polyethylene glycol (1.0-1.5 g/kg daily for ≥3 days) or a single dose of sodium picosulfate if polyethylene glycol was not feasible. Maintenance therapy with polyethylene glycol (0.5-0.8 g/kg daily) or magnesium hydroxide (500-1000 mg/d) was adjusted for response and tolerance. Stimulant laxatives (sodium picosulfate) or transanal irrigation were added as appropriate. Scheduled toileting after meals was performed 1 to 3 times daily. SU included education of the child and caregivers, instruction on optimal toilet posture, adequate fluid intake (1200-1500 mL/d), and timed voiding supported by a timer watch, usually every 2 hours. Adherence to bowel management was monitored in all participants, with laxative doses adjusted as needed through telephone consultations at weeks 2 and 4. In the SU arm, adherence to urotherapy was reinforced during these contacts. Outcomes were evaluated at week 12 and compared with baseline. Adverse events were recorded as part of routine clinical practice; no new interventions were introduced. Outcomes Primary End Point The primary outcome was the number of wet days per week, assessed by the Dry Pie bladder diary (eFigure in ). Participants, with age-appropriate assistance from caregivers, completed the diary for the week prior to each study visit. Each day was color-coded to reflect the most severe episode of incontinence. Treatment response was assessed by the estimated daily risk of a wet day, the expected number of wet days per week, and response rates according to ICCS guidelines, defined as follows: (1) no response (<50% reduction in the number of wet days), (2) partial response (50%-99% reduction in the number of wet days), and (3) complete response (100% reduction in the number of wet days [complete dryness during the diary week]). Secondary End Points Secondary outcomes included incontinence severity, bowel outcomes, and bladder function. Incontinence severity was quantified using a score derived from the Dry Pie diary. Each day was scored as follows: 0, dry day; 1, incontinence limited to wet underclothing; 2, wet clothes; and 3, wet socks. Bowel outcomes included stool consistency (Bristol Stool Scale), rectal diameter assessed by abdominal ultrasonography, and the number of fulfilled Rome IV criteria. Fecal incontinence was reported both within the Rome IV framework and as a separate outcome due to its clinical significance. Bladder function was assessed using frequency volume medical record–derived measures: daily voiding frequency and maximum voided volume relative to expected bladder capacity, considered a proxy for functional bladder volume. Post Hoc Analyses To evaluate the impact of bowel management on DUI, we pooled all participants irrespective of randomization and categorized according to bowel management outcome at follow-up: successful (<2 Rome IV criteria) and nonsuccessful (≥2 Rome IV criteria). The primary outcome, wet days per week, was analyzed both unadjusted and adjusted for baseline wet days. To evaluate the effect of adherence to urotherapy, we categorized participants in the SU arm into 3 adherence groups: full (n = 16), partial (n = 17), or none (n = 8). Adherence was assessed at visit 2 and during telephone follow-ups. Those who performed no urotherapy the week prior to visit 2 were considered nonadherent. Participants missing more than 1 alarm per day were partially adherent; those adhering during telephone follow-ups and missing 1 or fewer alarms per day at visit 2 were fully adherent. Statistical Analysis Sample size calculations were based on previously reported treatment response rates. , A total of 82 participants (41 per group) were required to detect a clinically meaningful difference in complete dryness rates with 80% power at a 2-sided α = .05. The final analyzed cohort included 83 participants; details are provided in the eMethods and eAppendix in . Baseline characteristics were summarized descriptively. Continuous variables were assessed for normality using Q-Q plots and reported as mean (SD) or median (IQR) as appropriate. Categorical variables were presented as numbers (percentages). Primary and secondary outcomes were analyzed in the modified intention-to-treat (mITT) population (all randomized participants with 12-week follow-up); participants with missing data were included in baseline summaries but excluded from analyses, without imputation. Daily risk of DUI was estimated using binomial regression with robust variance clustered by participant; from this, the expected number of wet days per week was derived. Effect estimates are reported as risk ratios and risk differences with 95% CIs. Response rates were compared using χ 2 tests, with relative risks (RRs) and 95% CIs. Incontinence severity scores were analyzed using analysis of covariance, with model assumptions evaluated by residual diagnostics; results are presented as adjusted mean differences with 95% CIs. No formal analyses of adverse events were performed; events were monitored as part of routine clinical care, and no unexpected or clinically significant events occurred. All analyses were performed in R, version 4.5.1 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing), with 2-sided P < .05 considered statistically significant. Eleven discontinued before end point assessment, leaving 83 for the mITT analysis. Reasons in the monotherapy group (n = 6) included withdrawal before starting treatment (n = 2), dissatisfaction with allocation (n = 1), spontaneous symptom resolution (n = 1), and missing follow-up data (n = 2). In the combination therapy group (n = 5), reasons included withdrawal before starting treatment (n = 2), clinical issues (positive urine culture result or hospital admission, n = 2), and missing follow-up data (n = 1). In the combination therapy group (n = 5), reasons included withdrawal before starting treatment (n = 2), clinical issues (positive urine culture result or hospital admission, n = 2), and missing follow-up data (n = 1). All 94 participants were included in the intention-to-treat (ITT) population for baseline characteristics, which were generally balanced ( ). Baseline characteristics for all populations, including ITT, mITT total, and mITT by treatment allocation, are given in eTable 2 in . No other concurrent interventions relevant to bowel or bladder function were administered during the study period. No unexpected or clinically significant adverse events occurred. Bowel Management At baseline, 83 of 94 participants (88.3%) received a bowel cleanout (polyethylene glycol or sodium picosulfate), 9 (9.6%) maintenance stool softeners only (polyethylene glycol or magnesium hydroxide), and 2 (2.1%) stimulant laxatives. At follow-up, 78 of 83 (94.0%) continued maintenance stool softeners, 5 (6.0%) used stimulant laxatives, and 9 (10.8%) received low-volume irrigation; some participants received combination treatments, explaining percentages exceeding 100% (eTable 3 in ). Interventions were delivered according to protocol, with high adherence to bowel management and variable adherence to SU as reported. Effect on DUI Model-based estimates showed that the daily risk of a wet day decreased from 0.75 (95% CI, 0.70-0.80) at baseline to 0.54 (95% CI, 0.44-0.65) in the monotherapy group and 0.55 (95% CI, 0.45-0.66) in the combination therapy group. The expected number of wet days per week decreased from 5.3 (95% CI, 4.9-5.6) to 3.8 (95% CI, 3.0-4.6) and 3.9 (95% CI, 3.1-4.6), respectively, with no between-group difference ( P = .92) ( and ). The number of participants achieving a 50% or greater reduction in the number of wet days per week was 16 (38.1%; 95% CI, 23.6%-54.4%) in the monotherapy group and 12 (29.3%; 95% CI, 16.1%-45.5%) in the combination therapy group, again with no between-group difference (RR, 0.88; 95% CI, 0.64-1.19; P = .54) ( and ). Complete response was achieved by 6 (14.3%; 95% CI, 5.4%-28.5%) in the monotherapy group and 4 (9.8%; 95% CI, 2.7%-23.1%) in the combination therapy group. Mean (SD) incontinence severity scores decreased from 8.2 (3.3) at baseline to 5.8 (4.4) at follow-up in the monotherapy group and from 7.6 (4.1) to 5.5 (3.9) in the combination therapy group. The estimated mean difference between groups at follow-up (combination therapy vs monotherapy) was –0.1 (95% CI, –0.7 to 0.5; P = .71). Other Bladder and Bowel Outcomes Secondary outcomes are listed in eTable 4 in . Fecal incontinence decreased, rectal diameter tended to reduce, whereas Bristol Stool Scale and voiding frequency remained stable. Fluid intake increased in SU participants, as expected. The maximum voided volume relative to expected bladder capacity tended to be lower at baseline in the monotherapy group, but differences were not significant. Urge prevalence showed minor changes. Impact of Successful Bowel Management At follow-up, children with constipation resolution had 3.44 wet days per week (95% CI, 2.72-4.16) compared with 4.15 wet days (95% CI, 3.39-4.91) in those without resolution ( ). After adjusting for baseline wet days, the adjusted mean difference was –0.89 wet days (95% CI, –1.94 to –0.05; P = .04), with an adjusted daily RR of 0.78 (95% CI, 0.61-0.99; P = .04). Unadjusted analyses showed no statistically significant effect (mean difference, –0.71; 95% CI, –1.76 to 0.34; RR, 0.83; 95% CI, 0.63-1.19). Adherence to SU At follow-up, the unadjusted daily risk of wet days was 0.52 (95% CI, 0.36-0.68) in the full adherence group, 0.66 (95% CI, 0.50-0.82) in the partial group, and 0.39 (95% CI, 0.17-0.61) in the no adherence group, with no group differing from monotherapy. Adjustment for baseline wet days did not change the findings. No unexpected or clinically significant adverse events occurred. Response rates in our trial were lower, likely reflecting the shorter follow-up (12 weeks vs ≥12 months in the study by Loening-Baucke et al and 4 months in the study by Borch et al ) and the inclusion of all children with constipation, whereas the study by Borch et al included only those successfully treated. Several mechanisms may underlie the association between bowel dysfunction and lower urinary tract symptoms. Mechanical factors, such as rectal distension and fecal impaction, may exert pressure on the bladder or alter the vesicourethral angle, provoking detrusor overactivity, urgency, or incomplete emptying. , Emerging evidence suggests a more complex interaction involving sensoneurologic pathways: rectal distension inhibits bladder contractions, and animal models demonstrate cross-talk between colonic and bladder innervation at the lumbosacral cord level. Central mechanisms are increasingly recognized. Children with BBD more frequently present with neuropsychiatric comorbidities, including attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder and affective disorders, , , , , and neuroimaging studies , implicate the frontal cortex and anterior cingulate gyrus in both continence control and executive function. These findings support the hypothesis that BBD may partly reflect altered central regulation rather than isolated bladder or bowel dysfunction. Our study cannot distinguish mechanical from sensorineural or central mechanisms. However, the modest treatment effect after 12 weeks may reflect the contribution of sensory and central disturbances, which may require a longer time to normalize, and may be more pronounced in children with neuropsychiatric comorbidities. , , , , , SU and BBD A substantial body of evidence supports the efficacy of SU in children with DUI. In a retrospective cohort of 240 children, 55% achieved continence with SU, increasing to 70% among those receiving timer-watch support. In a 12-week prospective trial using systematic timer-watch assistance, partial and full response rates were 60% and 30%, respectively. These estimates align with a 2018 meta-analysis, and several studies show that timer-watch assistance enhances SU effects. , SU has not been systematically studied in children with BBD outside concomitant bowel management, making it difficult to disentangle the effects of each intervention. In our trial, the addition of SU to bowel management did not confer an additional benefit. Several explanations are possible. First, bladder and bowel symptoms may arise from overlapping neural mechanisms rather than additive processes so that normalization of bowel function alone can suffice to improve continence. Second, persistent constipation may attenuate responsiveness to urotherapy because rectal distension and altered sensory pathways can reduce the efficacy of bladder training. These findings underscore the importance of adequately treating constipation as a prerequisite for optimizing the effect of SU. Third, despite randomization, children in the combination therapy group tended to have lower functional bladder volumes, potentially limiting the scope for improvement, consistent with the inverse relationship between bladder overactivity and response to SU. Adherence to SU Despite timer-watch support and telephone calls to ensure adherence, adherence to SU was suboptimal: 80.5% continued SU at follow-up, with only 39.0% reporting full adherence. In comparison, Hagstrøm et al reported adherence rates of 67% in children with DUI undergoing timer-watch–assisted urotherapy, a modality associated with higher adherence compared with urotherapy without a timer watch (RR, 2.97; 95% CI, 1.46-6.06). The current study did not demonstrate any differences in treatment responses according to SU adherence. Although not statistically significant, less severe DUI in children who discontinued SU suggests motivation may be lower among those with milder symptoms. Reduced adherence to SU among children with BBD compared with those with isolated DUI may also reflect the added treatment burden of managing both bowel and bladder regimens, the higher prevalence of psychiatric comorbidities, and possibly limited perceived efficacy of SU when constipation remains inadequately controlled. Limitations Limitations of this study include the relatively short 12-week follow-up and the lack of long-term outcomes. No untreated control group was included, because withholding bowel management for 12 weeks would have been unethical. Consequently, observed effects may partly reflect placebo, the natural history of DUI (which generally shows lower responses in comparable age groups ), or regression to the mean. Conclusions This RCT found that bowel management significantly reduced DUI in children with BBD and that adding SU at treatment initiation provided no additional benefit. This finding highlights that bowel management alone was an effective first-line intervention and may be a prerequisite for successful SU.
